questions.question: What is reactive programming, and when does it actually help in Java backends?
questions.title: Reactive Programming — Fundamentals, Backpressure, and When It Helps
questions.direct_answer: Reactive programming is **non-blocking, event-driven data flow with explicit backpressure**. Instead of one thread per request blocking on I/O, a small **event loop** handles thousands of concurrent operations through callbacks. The Java standard is **Reactive Streams** (`Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Subscription`, `Processor`), implemented by Project Reactor (Spring) and RxJava (Netflix). It helps when you have many concurrent I/O-bound operations, need streaming (SSE / WebSocket), or compose async flows with backpressure. It does **not** help CPU-bound work. In 2026 with **JDK 21 virtual threads**, many "we need reactive for scale" arguments soften — pick reactive for streaming and true async pipelines, virtual threads for blocking-code scale.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core reactive understanding; honest perspective on when reactive is worth the complexity vs virtual threads
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using reactive everywhere 'for scale'; blocking inside Mono/Flux; ignoring backpressure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Reactive Streams spec, backpressure strategies, Project Loom impact, debugging trade-offs, context propagation

sections.title: What Reactive Actually Is
sections.content:
Reactive programming in Java is the combination of three ideas — non-blocking I/O, asynchronous composition, and explicit backpressure. They make sense together; missing any one weakens the model.

**Non-blocking I/O.** Threads don't wait for responses. When an HTTP call is made, the thread returns to the pool; when the response arrives, a callback runs (potentially on a different thread). One event-loop thread can service thousands of in-flight operations.

**Asynchronous composition.** Operations chain via operators — `map`, `flatMap`, `zip`, `filter`, `onErrorResume`. You describe a pipeline declaratively; data flows once something subscribes.

**Backpressure.** Consumers tell producers how much they can handle. If a slow consumer can't keep up, producers slow down or buffer — explicitly, not by silent overflow. This is what distinguishes reactive from plain callback-based async.

**`Mono` and `Flux` are recipes, not values.** Nothing happens until something subscribes. They are *cold* by default. Contrast with `CompletableFuture`, which starts work immediately on creation.

sections.title: The Java Reactive Ecosystem
sections.content:
**Reactive Streams (the standard)**
- Specification adopted into JDK 9 as `java.util.concurrent.Flow`
- Four interfaces — `Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Subscription`, `Processor`
- Defines the contract for backpressure-aware async stream processing

**Project Reactor (Spring's implementation)**
- `Mono<T>` — 0 or 1 items
- `Flux<T>` — 0..N items
- Powers Spring WebFlux, R2DBC, Spring Data Reactive

**RxJava (Netflix's implementation)**
- `Observable`, `Single`, `Flowable`, `Completable`, `Maybe`
- Predates Reactor; widely used in Android and pre-Spring 5 services

**Spring stack components**
- `Spring WebFlux` — reactive web framework on Reactor Netty
- `WebClient` — reactive HTTP client
- `R2DBC` — reactive database drivers (Postgres, MySQL, MSSQL, H2)
- `Spring Data Reactive` — MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Neo4j, R2DBC

**RSocket**
- Binary application protocol; reactive-first
- Supports request-response, request-stream, channel, and fire-and-forget — all with backpressure

sections.title: Backpressure — The Key Differentiator
sections.content:
**The problem without backpressure** — a fast producer plus a slow consumer means memory explodes or events drop silently.

**Reactive Streams signals**
- `onSubscribe(subscription)` — consumer receives subscription handle
- `request(n)` — consumer asks for up to `n` items
- `onNext(item)` — producer delivers; repeats while demand remains
- `onComplete()` — terminal success signal
- `onError(t)` — terminal failure signal

The consumer controls pace by calling `request()`. The producer must not send more than requested. That contract is the heart of the spec.

**Backpressure strategies in Reactor**
- `onBackpressureBuffer(N)` — buffer up to `N` items; fail or drop when exceeded
- `onBackpressureDrop` — silently drop when downstream not ready
- `onBackpressureLatest` — keep only the latest
- `onBackpressureError` — signal an error if demand is exceeded

```java
Flux<String> stream = incomingEvents()
    .onBackpressureBuffer(1000, event -> log.warn("dropped: {}", event))
    .flatMap(this::processAsync, 8);
```

**Reactor concurrency parameter**
- `flatMap(fn, N)` processes up to `N` inner publishers concurrently
- This is your throttle — keep it bounded for I/O-bound work

**Hot vs cold publishers**
- **Cold** — produces from start on every subscription (e.g. `Flux.range(1, 10)`); each subscriber gets independent data
- **Hot** — events happen regardless of subscribers (websocket, sensor stream); late subscribers miss past events

**When backpressure isn't enough**
- For genuinely heterogeneous rates, insert a queue (Kafka, Reactor `Sinks`, RSocket)
- Monitor depth and alert on growth — backpressure inside one process can't fix a sustained mismatch

sections.title: Reactor in Practice
sections.content:
**Basic operators**

```java
Flux.range(1, 100)
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .map(n -> n * n)
    .take(5)
    .subscribe(System.out::println);   // 4, 16, 36, 64, 100
```

**Chaining async calls**
- `flatMap` for async transforms
- `Mono.zip` to wait for multiple async sources and combine results

```java
public Mono<OrderDTO> loadOrder(String id) {
    return orderRepo.findById(id)
        .flatMap(order -> Mono.zip(
            customerClient.getCustomer(order.customerId()),
            lineItemRepo.findByOrderId(order.id()).collectList())
            .map(t -> toDto(order, t.getT1(), t.getT2())))
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new OrderNotFound(id)));
}
```

**Error handling**
- `onStatus` for per-status policies
- `timeout`, `retryWhen` with backoff, `onErrorResume` for fallbacks

```java
client.post().uri("/charge").body(c)
    .retrieve()
    .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError,
              r -> Mono.error(new UpstreamException()))
    .bodyToMono(ChargeResult.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
    .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)))
    .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class,
                   e -> Mono.just(ChargeResult.deferred()));
```

**Reactor Context — the reactive ThreadLocal**
- Reactive streams cross threads; `ThreadLocal` and MDC don't carry automatically
- Use Reactor `Context` plus Micrometer Context Propagation in Boot 3.x

```java
return Mono.deferContextual(ctx ->
        Mono.just("tenant: " + ctx.get("tenant")))
    .contextWrite(Context.of("tenant", "acme"));
```

**Blocking call inside reactive — required pattern**
- Wrap with `Mono.fromCallable` and `subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())`
- Never block on an event-loop thread

```java
Mono.fromCallable(() -> jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(sql, Foo.class))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
```

sections.title: When Reactive Helps, When It Hurts, and What Loom Changes
sections.content:
**When reactive helps:**
- Thousands of concurrent slow I/O operations and limited threads
- Streaming endpoints — SSE, WebSocket, chunked HTTP, Kafka streaming
- Composing many async flows with per-step error handling
- Memory-constrained or container-limited environments
- Truly reactive downstream all the way (R2DBC, reactive HTTP, reactive broker)

**When reactive hurts:**
- CPU-bound workloads — reactive doesn't make CPU faster
- Blocking dependencies (plain JDBC, blocking SDKs) — wrapping with `boundedElastic` removes most of the benefit
- Inexperienced team — debugging stack traces, async timing, lost context are real
- Already on a thread-per-request model that isn't saturated

**Watch for — common mistakes:**
- **`.block()` in reactive code** — deadlocks or stalls the event loop
- **Ignoring backpressure** — fast producer + slow consumer = memory explosion
- **Blocking operations without `subscribeOn`** — event-loop stall halts every request
- **Loss of MDC and tracing context** — use Context Propagation
- **Forgetting to subscribe** — code looks correct but does nothing because publishers are cold
- **Mixing `CompletableFuture` and `Mono` carelessly** — eager vs lazy execution confusion

**Cost of reactive (be honest in interviews):**
- Debugging is harder — stack traces don't show the logical path
- `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` and `.checkpoint()` help in dev; turn off in prod (slow)
- Learning curve — operators, schedulers, context, backpressure take months
- Mixed reactive + blocking codebase is the worst case; one stray `.block()` negates the model
- Every dependency must be reactive for the model to pay off — JDBC, JMS, some SDKs are blocking

**Project Loom changes the calculus (JDK 21+):**
- Virtual threads — 10K-100K cheap threads per JVM; blocking I/O parks the virtual thread without blocking a platform thread
- Tomcat on virtual threads (Spring Boot 3.2+) — plain blocking code handles 10K+ concurrent connections with familiar code
- For "scale the blocking code" problems, virtual threads often win — simpler code, normal stack traces, fewer bugs

**Real numbers**
- Blocking Tomcat — ~200 threads serving I/O-bound requests = ~200 concurrent
- Netty reactive — 4 event-loop threads handling 10K+ concurrent
- Tomcat with virtual threads — 10K+ virtual threads, similar effective concurrency to reactive

**Observability:**
- Spring Boot auto-configures Micrometer metrics for Reactor
- `BlockHound` in tests detects accidental blocking on event-loop threads
- OpenTelemetry / Micrometer Tracing has Reactor Context propagation support

**The 2026 recommendation:**
- Default to **Spring MVC + virtual threads** for new services
- Use **Spring WebFlux** when streaming, RSocket, or reactive-all-the-way is a genuine requirement
- Don't mix blocking and reactive — pick one stance per service

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reactive = non-blocking I/O + async composition + explicit backpressure**
- **Reactive Streams** standard — `Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Subscription`; Reactor and RxJava implement it
- **`Mono` (0..1) and `Flux` (0..N)** are cold by default — nothing runs without subscribe
- **Backpressure** is the differentiator from plain callbacks — consumer controls pace
- **Reactive helps** for thousands of concurrent I/O, streaming, async composition
- **Doesn't help** CPU-bound work, blocking dependencies, inexperienced teams
- **Never block on event-loop thread** — `subscribeOn(boundedElastic)` for blocking calls
- **Context propagation** replaces ThreadLocal / MDC across threads
- **Project Loom virtual threads** make reactive-for-scale less compelling in 2026
- **2026 default** — Spring MVC + virtual threads; pick WebFlux for streaming or reactive-all-the-way

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Reactive programming is non-blocking, event-driven data flow with explicit backpressure. Instead of one thread per request blocking on I/O, a small event loop handles thousands of concurrent operations via callbacks.

**Three core ideas**
- Non-blocking I/O — threads don't wait; callback on response
- Async composition — operators chain declaratively (`map`, `flatMap`, `zip`, `filter`)
- Backpressure — consumers tell producers how much they can handle

**Java ecosystem**
- Reactive Streams standard — `java.util.concurrent.Flow`
- Project Reactor (Spring) — `Mono` for 0..1, `Flux` for 0..N
- RxJava — `Observable`, `Single`, `Flowable`, `Completable`, `Maybe`
- Spring WebFlux on Reactor Netty
- R2DBC reactive DB drivers; Spring Data Reactive for MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra
- RSocket for reactive RPC

**`Mono` and `Flux` are recipes, not values**
- Cold by default; nothing runs until subscribe
- Contrast `CompletableFuture` which starts immediately

**Backpressure differentiator**
- Signals — `onSubscribe`, `request(n)`, `onNext`, `onComplete`, `onError`
- Reactor strategies — `onBackpressureBuffer/Drop/Latest/Error`
- `flatMap(fn, N)` concurrency parameter is your throttle
- Hot vs cold publishers — late subscribers miss hot events

**Reactor in practice**
- `flatMap` for async; `Mono.zip` for parallel composition
- Error handling — `onStatus`, `timeout`, `retryWhen` with backoff, `onErrorResume`
- Reactor `Context` is the reactive ThreadLocal
- Wrap blocking calls — `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())`

**When reactive helps**
- Thousands of concurrent slow I/O
- Streaming — SSE, WebSocket, chunked HTTP, Kafka
- Reactive downstream all the way
- Memory-constrained environments

**When reactive does NOT help**
- CPU-bound workload
- Blocking dependency (plain JDBC, blocking SDK)
- Team without reactive experience
- Service already healthy on thread-per-request

**Common mistakes**
- `.block()` in reactive code — deadlocks or stalls
- Ignoring backpressure — memory explosion
- Blocking without `subscribeOn` — event-loop stall
- Loss of MDC / tracing — use Context Propagation
- Forgetting to subscribe — code does nothing

**Project Loom changes the calculus (JDK 21+)**
- Virtual threads — 10K-100K cheap threads per JVM
- Tomcat on virtual threads handles 10K+ concurrent with simple blocking code
- For "scale the blocking code" problems, virtual threads often win

**2026 recommendation**
- Default — Spring MVC + virtual threads
- WebFlux when streaming or reactive-all-the-way is a real requirement
- Don't mix blocking and reactive in one service

**Strategic answer**
- Reactive is about non-blocking, composition, and backpressure
- Not a universal scaling magic bullet
- Great for streaming and truly async pipelines
- Virtual threads cover the "just scale my blocking code" case in 2026
- Pick reactive when streaming or reactive-all-the-way genuinely fits

questions.question: Imperative vs reactive — how does the mental model actually differ?
questions.title: Imperative vs Reactive — The Mental Model Shift
questions.direct_answer: Imperative code executes **eagerly, sequentially, on the calling thread** — `var users = userService.findAll(); var orders = ordersFor(users);` runs each line in order, blocking until each result arrives. Reactive code is **declarative and lazy** — `userService.findAll().flatMap(this::ordersFor)` builds a pipeline description; nothing runs until something subscribes, and execution happens **whenever data is ready, on whatever thread the scheduler chose**. The shift is mostly mental: from "do this, then this" to "describe a pipeline, hand it off, react to signals." Errors are signals not exceptions, threads are not yours, and `ThreadLocal` doesn't survive across operator boundaries. This change is why reactive code looks elegant in slides and confusing in real production logs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can articulate the cognitive shift required for reactive — beyond just operator names
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Mono / Flux like blocking values; expecting try/catch and ThreadLocal to work; assuming order-of-execution from line order
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss eager vs lazy evaluation, thread-of-execution unpredictability, error-as-signal vs error-as-exception, and how virtual threads keep the imperative model viable

sections.title: Two Models, Two Mental Pictures
sections.content:
The deepest difference between imperative and reactive code is not the operator names — it is the **mental picture of how a piece of code runs**.

**Imperative is eager, sequential, calling-thread.** You write `var users = service.findAll()` and the calling thread blocks until the result is back.
- Then `var orders = ordersFor(users)` runs.
- The order of operations matches the order of lines.
- Errors are exceptions that propagate up the stack. `ThreadLocal` works because the same thread runs every line.
- Stack traces show exactly the path that produced an error.

**Reactive is declarative, lazy, scheduler-driven.** You write `service.findAll().flatMap(this::ordersFor)` and you have built a *description* of work, not done it.
- Nothing runs until something subscribes.
- Once subscribed, execution happens whenever data is ready, on whatever thread the scheduler picks.
- Errors are signals that travel down the chain, not exceptions that travel up the call stack. `ThreadLocal` doesn't survive across operator boundaries — you need Reactor `Context`.

The surface syntax is similar enough that engineers underestimate the cognitive shift. Reactive looks like a sequence of method calls, but it isn't. Treating it like imperative is the source of almost every reactive bug.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Mental Model
sections.content:
Each row shows where the assumption from imperative breaks down in reactive — and how virtual threads keep most of the imperative model viable.

| Aspect | Imperative | Reactive | Imperative on Virtual Threads |
|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation | Eager — runs immediately | Lazy — runs on subscribe | Eager — runs immediately |
| Order of execution | Top-to-bottom on calling thread | Determined by data arrival and scheduler | Top-to-bottom on virtual thread |
| Thread of execution | Same thread throughout | May switch on every operator | One virtual thread throughout |
| Errors | Exceptions, propagate up stack | Signals, propagate down chain | Exceptions, propagate up stack |
| `try` / `catch` | Works | Doesn't catch reactive signals | Works |
| `ThreadLocal` / MDC | Works | Doesn't carry across operators | Works (with care) |
| `@Transactional` | Works | Needs reactive tx manager | Works |
| Stack traces | Show full call path | Truncated; need `checkpoint()` | Show full call path |
| Backpressure | None in-process | Native | None in-process |
| Concurrency limit | Thread pool size | Event-loop + flatMap concurrency | Virtual-thread-cheap |
| Composing async | `CompletableFuture.thenCompose` | `flatMap` with operators | Plain blocking calls |
| Learning curve | Low | High | Low |

sections.title: Same Logic in Both Styles
Where the Mental Model Breaks for Beginners
sections.content:
Five places where reactive consistently surprises people coming from imperative.

**1. Lazy evaluation**
- `Mono.just(expensiveCall())` runs `expensiveCall()` *immediately* — `Mono.just` only takes the value
- For lazy evaluation, use `Mono.fromCallable(() -> expensiveCall())`
- A `Mono` with no subscriber does nothing — including no logging

**2. Threads change**
- Operators may run on different threads depending on `subscribeOn` / `publishOn`
- A line of code might run on the Netty event-loop, the parallel scheduler, or `boundedElastic` — sometimes all in one chain
- `ThreadLocal` set before the chain doesn't survive into operators

**3. Errors are signals, not exceptions**
- `try / catch` around a reactive call catches nothing — the error happens later
- Use `onErrorResume`, `onErrorReturn`, `onErrorMap` inside the chain
- An unhandled error terminates the sequence; subsequent items never arrive

**4. Order of execution is not order of lines**
- `.doOnNext(...)` doesn't "happen now" — it's wired in for later
- Side effects in operators may run interleaved across items
- Logging order in production differs from what your code looks like

**5. `@Transactional` doesn't just work**
- Spring's `@Transactional` is `ThreadLocal`-bound — works fine in imperative
- Reactive needs `R2dbcTransactionManager` and reactive operations through the chain
- Mixing blocking and reactive across a transaction is a footgun

sections.title: Cognitive Cost vs Power, and How Virtual Threads Change It
sections.content:
**When the reactive mental model pays off:**
- Streaming pipelines where backpressure is a first-class concern
- Composing many parallel async calls in one expression
- Truly reactive downstream all the way through
- Memory-efficient processing of huge data streams

**When the cost outweighs the benefit:**
- Standard CRUD with blocking dependencies — wrapping in `boundedElastic` removes most of the benefit and keeps all of the cost
- Team without months of reactive experience — debugging cost is real
- Workloads that don't actually need extreme concurrency
- CPU-bound code — reactive doesn't help

**Watch for in production:**
- **Stack traces lose context** — use `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` in dev (slow; turn off in prod) and `.checkpoint("label")` in chains
- **Logging order is misleading** — reactive logs tell you what happened, not in code order
- **Memory hot spots** — `collectList()` on unbounded `Flux`, `onBackpressureBuffer` without bound
- **Lost MDC** — Spring Boot 3.x bridges via Micrometer Context Propagation, but you must enable it
- **Mixed blocking and reactive** — every `.block()` or unwrapped JDBC call defeats the model

**How virtual threads change the picture:**
- The original argument for reactive was "scale beyond thread-per-request" — virtual threads cover that case while keeping the imperative mental model
- For most services in 2026, **MVC + virtual threads + blocking JDBC** scales to 10K+ connections with code that any Java developer can read, debug, and profile
- Reactive remains the right answer when streaming, RSocket, explicit backpressure, or reactive-all-the-way are real requirements — not just when you want concurrency

**Strategic guidance:**
- Don't pick reactive for the operators alone — pick it because the problem genuinely is event-driven and async
- If you find yourself fighting reactive (10+ operator chains, `.block()` everywhere, debugger pain), reconsider whether virtual threads fit better
- Mixed reactive + blocking codebases are the worst of both worlds — pick one stance per service
- Treat reactive as an investment in a different mental model, not a syntactic preference

sections.content:
- **Imperative** is eager, sequential, single-thread; **reactive** is lazy, declarative, scheduler-driven
- **Reactive code is a description** — nothing runs until subscribe
- **Errors are signals** in reactive — `try/catch` doesn't catch them
- **Threads change** across operators — `ThreadLocal` and MDC don't survive without Reactor `Context`
- **Order of execution is not order of lines** — `.doOnNext` runs later, possibly interleaved
- **Stack traces lose context** — use `.checkpoint()` and `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` in dev
- **`@Transactional` doesn't just work** — needs reactive tx manager and reactive chain
- **Virtual threads keep the imperative model viable** at reactive-like concurrency
- **Pick reactive for genuine event-driven async** — not for syntactic preference
- **Don't mix blocking and reactive** in one service if you can avoid it

| Aspect | Imperative | Reactive | Imperative on Virtual Threads | |---|---|---|---| | Evaluation | Eager — runs immediately | Lazy — runs on subscribe | Eager — runs immediately | | Order of execution | Top-to-bottom on calling thread | Determined by data arrival and scheduler | Top-to-bottom on virtual thread | | Thread of execution | Same thread throughout | May switch on every operator | One virtual thread throughout | | Errors | Exceptions, propagate up stack | Signals, propagate down chain | Exceptions, propagate up stack | | try / catch | Works | Doesn't catch reactive signals | Works | | ThreadLocal / MDC | Works | Doesn't carry across operators | Works (with care) | | @Transactional | Works | Needs reactive tx manager | Works | | Stack traces | Show full call path | Truncated; need checkpoint() | Show full call path | | Backpressure | None in-process | Native | None in-process | | Concurrency limit | Thread pool size | Event-loop + flatMap concurrency | Virtual-thread-cheap | | Composing async | CompletableFuture
thenCompose | flatMap with operators | Plain blocking calls | | Learning curve | Low | High | Low |

beats.text: When the reactive mental model pays off: Streaming pipelines where backpressure is a first-class concern Composing many parallel async calls in one expression Truly reactive downstream all the way through Memory-efficient processing of huge data streams When the cost outweighs the benefit: Standard CRUD with blocking dependencies — wrapping in boundedElastic removes most of the benefit and keeps all of the cost Team without months of reactive experience — debugging cost is real Workloads that don't actually need extreme concurrency CPU-bound code — reactive doesn't help Watch for in production.

The deepest difference between imperative and reactive code is not the operator names — it is the mental picture of how a piece of code runs. Imperative is eager, sequential, calling-thread. You write var users = service.findAll() and the calling thread blocks until the result is back. Then var orders = ordersFor(users) runs. The order of operations matches the order.
